title: GERD: Treat the Typical Syndrome, Investigate the Alarm Features
bottomLine: Typical heartburn/regurgitation without alarm features can often be managed clinically with lifestyle measures and an appropriate PPI trial; dysphagia, GI bleeding, anemia, persistent vomiting, weight loss or other alarm features change the pathway to investigation rather than repeated empiric acid suppression.
recognize: Heartburn and acid regurgitation are the most typical symptoms; cough, chest discomfort and laryngeal symptoms are less specific.
Nocturnal/postprandial symptoms, obesity, hiatal hernia and selected medications can increase reflux burden.
differentiate: Cardiac ischemia must be considered before labelling exertional or high-risk chest pain reflux.
Eosinophilic esophagitis, peptic stricture, malignancy and motility disorders are important causes of dysphagia and should not be masked by indefinite PPI refills.
assessment: Characterize symptoms, dysphagia/odynophagia, bleeding, weight loss, vomiting, anemia risk, chest-pain features, pregnancy, NSAIDs and prior response to therapy.
workup: Typical uncomplicated GERD usually does not need immediate endoscopy.
Use upper endoscopy for alarm features or other guideline indications; reflux monitoring is useful when diagnosis remains uncertain or symptoms persist despite optimized therapy.
management: Use lifestyle measures targeted to the patient's triggers and appropriate PPI therapy; optimize timing/adherence before declaring treatment failure.
Step down to the lowest effective long-term strategy when clinically appropriate, while maintaining therapy when a clear chronic indication exists.
medicationSafety: Do not stop a clearly indicated PPI solely because of weak observational associations; periodically confirm indication and dose.
Consider interactions and magnesium/B12/renal or infection issues only when the clinical context warrants them rather than ordering routine broad monitoring for every user.
counselling: Explain meal timing, trigger-specific changes, weight/position strategies where relevant and correct PPI timing.
followUp: Reassess persistent symptoms and confirm whether the problem is ongoing reflux, adherence, another esophageal diagnosis or functional symptoms.
examTrap: Escalating acid suppression indefinitely in a patient with progressive dysphagia instead of arranging diagnostic evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Typical GERD can be treated empirically; alarm features earn an explanation.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology upper-GI guidance

title: Peptic Ulcer and H. pylori: Identify the Cause, Eradicate, Prove Cure
bottomLine: Peptic ulcer disease requires attention to H. pylori, NSAID/aspirin exposure and complications. When H. pylori is treated, eradication must be confirmed with an appropriate test after therapy; symptom improvement is not proof of cure.
recognize: Epigastric pain, dyspepsia, occult/overt bleeding or iron deficiency can occur; many ulcers are asymptomatic until a complication.
H. pylori and NSAIDs are major causes, but malignancy and other etiologies matter in selected ulcers.
differentiate: Perforation causes sudden severe pain/peritonitis; active upper-GI bleeding causes hematemesis/melena and may present with shock.
Functional dyspepsia lacks an explanatory structural lesion after appropriate evaluation.
assessment: Assess bleeding, hemodynamics, NSAIDs/ASA/anticoagulants, prior H. pylori treatment/antibiotic exposure, smoking/alcohol, cancer risk and pregnancy.
workup: Use urea breath or stool antigen testing for noninvasive active-infection testing when appropriate; serology does not confirm eradication.
Endoscopy is required for bleeding/alarm features and selected gastric-ulcer contexts.
management: Use an evidence-based eradication regimen chosen with current local resistance/previous antibiotic exposure and complete acid suppression as indicated.
Stop avoidable ulcerogenic NSAIDs; if antiplatelet/NSAID therapy is essential, manage gastroprotection and cardiovascular/bleeding risk together.
medicationSafety: PPI and antibiotic timing affect test-of-cure accuracy; follow the validated washout interval before urea-breath/stool testing.
Penicillin allergy and prior macrolide exposure can materially change regimen choice.
redFlags: Hemodynamic instability or major GI bleed
Unexplained weight loss or malignancy concern
counselling: Teach medication completion and why a post-treatment test is needed even when symptoms resolve.
followUp: Confirm H. pylori eradication and close the loop on gastric-ulcer healing/biopsy follow-up when indicated.
examTrap: Documenting H. pylori as cured because dyspepsia improved after treatment without performing a test of eradication.
oneLinePearl: Treat H. pylori, then prove it is gone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology H. pylori guidance

title: Dyspepsia: Alarm Features, H. pylori, Then Functional Management
bottomLine: Dyspepsia is an upper-GI symptom complex, not a diagnosis. Identify alarm features and medication causes, use age/risk-appropriate H. pylori testing or endoscopy, and treat functional dyspepsia only after important structural disease is reasonably excluded.
recognize: Postprandial fullness, early satiety and epigastric pain/burning are common dyspeptic symptoms.
NSAIDs, iron, bisphosphonates and other drugs can contribute.
differentiate: Biliary/pancreatic disease, cardiac ischemia and GERD can mimic dyspepsia.
Weight loss, anemia, progressive dysphagia, recurrent vomiting or bleeding are not routine functional dyspepsia.
assessment: Assess symptom pattern/duration, alarm features, NSAIDs/ASA, family history, H. pylori exposure/treatment, cardiac risk and diet/alcohol without over-attributing symptoms to food.
workup: Use H. pylori test-and-treat in appropriate lower-risk patients and endoscopy for alarm/high-risk presentations according to current guidance.
Avoid broad abdominal imaging for uncomplicated dyspepsia without a differential that imaging can answer.
management: Treat identified H. pylori; use PPI therapy and then evidence-based functional dyspepsia options when structural disease is not found.
Address medication causes and support nutrition without overly restrictive elimination diets.
medicationSafety: Long-term prokinetic/neuromodulator choices require agent-specific adverse-effect review; avoid chronic NSAIDs where ulcer risk is relevant.
counselling: Explain that functional dyspepsia is a real gut–brain interaction disorder after appropriate evaluation, not 'nothing wrong'.
followUp: Reassess failed empiric therapy and evolving alarm features rather than repeating the same prescription indefinitely.
examTrap: Calling dyspepsia functional before checking for H. pylori, ulcerogenic medication use and alarm features.
oneLinePearl: Dyspepsia is a symptom pathway: risk first, H. pylori/structure second, functional treatment third.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Dyspepsia Guideline

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Confirm Inflammation, Define Extent, Treat to Control Disease
bottomLine: IBD is not diagnosed from chronic diarrhea alone. Establish inflammatory disease with stool/lab/endoscopic evidence, distinguish Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis, assess severity/extraintestinal complications and coordinate steroid-sparing maintenance therapy with gastroenterology.
recognize: Bloody diarrhea/urgency is common in UC; Crohn disease can cause abdominal pain, weight loss, perianal disease, strictures/fistulas and small-bowel disease.
Arthritis, uveitis, skin disease, anemia and hepatobiliary disease can be extraintestinal manifestations.
differentiate: IBS does not produce objective intestinal inflammation, bleeding or weight loss.
Infection including C. difficile can mimic/trigger an IBD flare and should be considered before simply escalating immunosuppression.
assessment: Assess stool frequency/blood, nocturnal symptoms, pain, weight, fever, hydration, perianal disease, extraintestinal symptoms, medications/NSAIDs, smoking, pregnancy and prior therapy.
workup: Use CBC/iron/CRP and fecal calprotectin when clinically useful, stool infection testing in appropriate flares, and ileocolonoscopy with biopsies for diagnosis/extent; image small bowel/complications as indicated.
management: Match induction and maintenance therapy to disease type, extent and severity; corticosteroids are induction/rescue tools, not maintenance therapy.
Escalate severe colitis, obstruction, abscess, perforation, toxic megacolon or major bleeding urgently.
medicationSafety: Biologics/small molecules/immunomodulators require infection/vaccine, pregnancy and laboratory safety planning.
Avoid reflex NSAIDs when they worsen disease and review thrombosis risk during active severe IBD.
counselling: Discuss adherence, smoking cessation in Crohn disease, vaccination/infection precautions, nutrition and pregnancy planning with IBD therapy.
followUp: Treat to objective disease control and monitor cancer surveillance/complications according to extent/duration and therapy.
examTrap: Escalating steroids for presumed flare without considering C. difficile or another enteric infection.
oneLinePearl: IBD needs objective inflammation and a steroid-sparing maintenance plan.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology IBD guidelines/current library

title: IBS: Make a Positive Diagnosis After a Focused Red-Flag Screen
bottomLine: IBS can be diagnosed positively from a characteristic recurrent abdominal-pain/stool pattern after a focused screen for alarm features and appropriate limited testing. Do not force patients through endless exclusion testing when the presentation is typical and stable.
recognize: Recurrent abdominal pain associated with defecation and change in stool frequency/form is the core pattern; classify constipation-, diarrhea-, mixed- or unclassified subtype.
Bloating is common but nonspecific.
differentiate: GI bleeding, anemia, weight loss, nocturnal progressive symptoms, fever, family history of colorectal cancer/IBD/celiac or late/new atypical presentation requires a different pathway.
IBD/celiac/microscopic colitis and medication effects can mimic IBS-D.
assessment: Assess stool pattern, pain relationship, alarm features, diet, medications, pelvic-floor symptoms, stress/mental health and impact on function without suggesting symptoms are imaginary.
workup: Use targeted CBC/celiac serology and inflammatory testing when indicated by subtype/risk; avoid routine colonoscopy/imaging in younger low-risk typical IBS without alarm features.
management: Use subtype-directed diet/fibre, antispasmodic/constipation/diarrhea therapies and gut-brain interventions; a structured low-FODMAP trial should include reintroduction/personalization rather than permanent maximal restriction.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic opioid therapy for IBS pain and review anticholinergic/sedating burden where relevant.
redFlags: New significant symptoms in a higher-risk older patient
counselling: Use a positive diagnosis and explain the gut–brain interaction; avoid 'all tests normal so nothing is wrong' messaging.
followUp: Track symptom/function goals and reconsider diagnosis when the pattern changes or treatment repeatedly fails.
examTrap: Ordering repeated CT/colonoscopy for a stable classic IBS pattern with no alarm features instead of making a positive diagnosis and treating the subtype.
oneLinePearl: IBS is a positive clinical diagnosis after a focused safety screen, not a diagnosis of exhausted testing.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology IBS guideline/current resources

title: Celiac Disease: Test While Gluten Is Still in the Diet
bottomLine: Celiac disease requires appropriate serology while the patient is consuming gluten, followed by specialist/biopsy confirmation according to age and pathway. Starting a gluten-free diet before testing can make diagnosis harder and should not be the default diagnostic trial.
recognize: Diarrhea, bloating, weight loss, iron deficiency, osteoporosis, transaminitis, dermatitis herpetiformis and extraintestinal presentations can occur.
Risk is higher with type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, first-degree family history and selected genetic syndromes.
differentiate: Non-celiac gluten sensitivity and wheat allergy are different diagnoses.
IgA deficiency can cause a false-negative standard IgA tissue-transglutaminase test and requires an IgG-based strategy.
assessment: Confirm current gluten exposure, symptoms, anemia/bone disease, autoimmune disease, family history and prior self-imposed dietary restriction.
workup: Use tTG-IgA plus total IgA as the standard initial adult strategy when appropriate; use IgG-based tests if IgA deficient and refer for endoscopic duodenal biopsy/diagnostic confirmation according to current pathway.
management: Use a strict lifelong gluten-free diet after diagnosis with dietitian support and correct iron, folate/B12, vitamin D/calcium or other deficiencies.
Assess bone health and associated autoimmune disease according to risk.
medicationSafety: Check excipients/supplements only when clinically relevant; do not replace dietary treatment with unproven supplements or enzymes.
redFlags: Persistent symptoms despite verified gluten-free diet
GI bleeding/weight loss raising malignancy or alternate diagnosis
counselling: Teach cross-contact/label reading and that testing family members may be appropriate; avoid requiring dietary restriction before diagnosis is established.
followUp: Monitor clinical response, nutritional deficiencies and celiac serology as useful; persistent disease requires adherence and alternate/refractory diagnosis review.
examTrap: Telling a patient to stop gluten for several months before ordering celiac serology.
oneLinePearl: For celiac diagnosis, gluten exposure makes the test interpretable.

title: Hepatitis B and C: Confirm Active Infection, Stage Liver Risk, Link to Curative or Suppressive Therapy
bottomLine: HBV and HCV testing answer different questions. For HCV, reactive antibody requires RNA to confirm current infection; for HBV, interpret HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc and HBV DNA together. Link active disease to current Canadian treatment and fibrosis/HCC pathways rather than using ALT alone.
recognize: Chronic HBV/HCV can be asymptomatic until advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis; thrombocytopenia or abnormal liver chemistry may be the first clue.
Pregnancy, immunosuppression and coinfection change urgency and prophylaxis/treatment decisions.
differentiate: HCV antibody indicates exposure, not necessarily current infection; HCV RNA confirms active infection.
HBsAg positivity, isolated core antibody and vaccine immunity have different meanings and should not be collapsed into 'positive hepatitis B'.
assessment: Assess transmission risk, prior tests/treatment, country of origin, pregnancy, alcohol/substances, HIV/other hepatitis, immunosuppression, liver decompensation and medication access.
workup: For HCV use antibody then reflex/confirmatory RNA and assess fibrosis/liver disease; genotype testing is regimen-context dependent in the modern DAA era.
For HBV use complete serology, HBV DNA, ALT/liver assessment and stage fibrosis/HCC risk; test coinfections as indicated.
management: Consider all chronic HCV patients for curative direct-acting antiviral therapy, generally through an experienced prescriber/program; current courses are usually short and highly effective.

Use CASL/AMMI 2025 HBV criteria to decide who needs antiviral treatment, monitoring or prophylaxis during immunosuppression; pregnancy may require specialist antiviral planning to reduce transmission.
medicationSafety: Check renal/hepatic function and drug interactions for DAA/NUC therapy.
Before immunosuppressive/anti-CD20 therapy, recognize HBV reactivation risk even in some HBsAg-negative/anti-HBc-positive patients and arrange prophylaxis/monitoring.
counselling: Explain reinfection after HCV cure is possible and review HBV/HCV transmission, vaccination for other hepatitis where appropriate and alcohol/liver-health counseling.
followUp: Confirm HCV sustained virologic response and continue HCC surveillance when cirrhosis remains; maintain HBV treatment/monitoring/HCC surveillance according to stage.
examTrap: Calling a reactive HCV antibody current infection without checking HCV RNA—or starting immunosuppression without addressing HBV reactivation risk.
oneLinePearl: HCV antibody finds exposure, HCV RNA finds current infection; HBV needs the whole serologic/DNA pattern.
sourceBasis: PHAC Hepatitis C for Health Professionals updated 2025
PHAC Hepatitis B for Health Professionals updated 2025

title: MASLD: Identify Fibrosis Risk, Treat Cardiometabolic Disease
bottomLine: The canonical Full identity uses the older NAFLD term, but current learner-facing care uses metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). The priority is fibrosis risk and cardiometabolic treatment—not proving steatosis repeatedly or following ALT alone.
recognize: MASLD is strongly associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension and sleep apnea; aminotransferases can be normal despite significant fibrosis.
Cardiovascular disease is a major source of morbidity/mortality in MASLD.
differentiate: Exclude clinically important alcohol exposure and other liver diseases rather than assuming every fatty liver is metabolic.
Simple steatosis and advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis require different follow-up intensity.
assessment: Assess metabolic risk, alcohol, medications, viral hepatitis risk, sleep apnea, family history and signs of advanced liver disease.
workup: Use noninvasive fibrosis risk assessment such as FIB-4 followed by elastography/specialist evaluation when risk is elevated; ultrasound can identify steatosis but does not stage fibrosis reliably.
management: Treat diabetes, obesity, BP, dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk aggressively; use evidence-based weight-management pharmacotherapy/metabolic surgery when indicated and coordinate hepatology for significant fibrosis.
Do not withhold indicated statins simply because MASLD is present.
medicationSafety: Review hepatotoxic medications clinically, but avoid unnecessary cessation of beneficial cardiometabolic therapy from mild stable aminotransferase elevation alone.
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing metabolic-health language and explain that normal ALT does not prove low liver risk.
followUp: Repeat fibrosis risk assessment at an interval based on metabolic risk and initial results; advanced fibrosis needs cirrhosis/HCC pathways.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient with diabetes and fatty liver because ALT is normal instead of assessing fibrosis risk.
oneLinePearl: In MASLD, fibrosis—not fat alone—determines liver prognosis.
sourceBasis: CASL steatotic liver disease resources/current nomenclature

title: Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease: Diagnose the Stage, Treat Alcohol Use and Liver Risk Together
bottomLine: Alcohol-associated liver disease ranges from steatosis to hepatitis and cirrhosis. Quantify alcohol use nonjudgmentally, assess withdrawal/nutrition and liver severity, treat alcohol use disorder as part of liver care, and urgently escalate severe hepatitis or decompensation.
recognize: AST/ALT pattern can support but never prove alcohol as the cause; jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, fever and systemic inflammation can occur in alcohol-associated hepatitis.
Malnutrition, infection, pancreatitis, GI bleeding and withdrawal commonly coexist.
differentiate: Viral, autoimmune, metabolic and drug-related liver injury can coexist with alcohol exposure.
Alcohol-associated hepatitis is a clinical severity syndrome, not simply elevated AST after drinking.
assessment: Use a non-stigmatizing alcohol history, last drink/withdrawal risk, nutrition, medications, infection/GI bleeding, pancreatitis, mental health and social supports; assess decompensation.
workup: Use CBC, electrolytes/renal function, liver chemistry, INR, bilirubin and cause-directed testing; calculate validated severity scores when alcohol-associated hepatitis is suspected and treatment decisions depend on them.
management: Abstinence/reduction support and evidence-based AUD treatment are central; manage withdrawal safely, correct nutrition/thiamine risk and treat cirrhosis complications.
Severe alcohol-associated hepatitis requires hospital/specialty evaluation; corticosteroid eligibility requires careful infection/GI bleeding/renal and severity assessment.
medicationSafety: AUD medications require liver/renal context; avoid assuming all pharmacotherapy is contraindicated because liver disease exists.
Sedatives used for withdrawal require monitored dosing, especially with encephalopathy/respiratory risk.
counselling: Use respectful language, offer AUD treatment rather than 'just stop drinking', and involve addiction/hepatology services when appropriate.
followUp: Track alcohol-use goals, liver recovery/fibrosis and cirrhosis/HCC surveillance when indicated.
examTrap: Attributing every abnormal liver test to alcohol and missing viral hepatitis, obstruction or acetaminophen toxicity—or offering abstinence advice without AUD treatment.
oneLinePearl: Treat the liver disease and the alcohol use disorder as one care plan.

title: Cirrhosis: Find Decompensation, Prevent the Next Event
bottomLine: Cirrhosis care is complication surveillance and prevention: ascites/SBP, variceal bleeding, encephalopathy, renal dysfunction, malnutrition and HCC. New decompensation is a change in prognosis and usually warrants hepatology/transplant consideration rather than another routine outpatient visit.
recognize: Ascites, variceal bleed, hepatic encephalopathy and jaundice are major decompensation events.
Thrombocytopenia, sarcopenia, edema and portal-hypertension findings may precede overt decompensation.
differentiate: A high ammonia level alone does not diagnose or stage hepatic encephalopathy.
AKI in cirrhosis may be hypovolemia, infection, nephrotoxicity, ATN or hepatorenal physiology and requires evaluation before assuming HRS.
assessment: Assess mental status, bleeding, infection, ascites/edema, renal function/urine, medications including NSAIDs/diuretics/sedatives, nutrition, alcohol, vaccination and prior variceal/HCC screening.
workup: Diagnostic paracentesis is indicated for new/worsening ascites and hospitalized decompensation where SBP must be excluded; use CBC, renal/electrolytes, bilirubin/INR and cause-directed testing.
Use guideline-based variceal and HCC surveillance rather than tumour markers alone.
management: Treat the specific complication: sodium/diuretic strategy and paracentesis for ascites, antibiotics/albumin protocols for SBP, vasoactive/endoscopic pathway for acute variceal bleeding, lactulose±rifaximin for recurrent overt encephalopathy, and urgent cause-directed AKI care.
Refer decompensated patients for hepatology/transplant assessment when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine NSAIDs; sedatives/opioids can precipitate encephalopathy/falls; diuretics require sodium/potassium/renal monitoring.
Do not correct INR/platelets routinely before every low-risk procedure solely to normalize numbers.
counselling: Teach when confusion, fever, GI bleeding, falling urine output or rapid abdominal swelling requires urgent care; include nutrition and alcohol treatment.
followUp: Close the loop on variceal/HCC surveillance, decompensation prevention, transplant candidacy and medication monitoring.
examTrap: Using an ammonia level to decide whether confusion is hepatic encephalopathy instead of evaluating precipitants and alternative causes.
oneLinePearl: Every cirrhosis visit asks: has this patient decompensated, and how do we prevent the next event?
